# Exercise 2.2 — First look {#sec-first-look}


:::: {.web-only}
Every cell on this page is a real R or Python cell. Open `day2-01-first-look.qmd`
in your editor and run them one at a time — the output printed here is what you
should get. If a package is missing, run `source("scripts/setup_local.R")` once and
restart R.
::::

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Describe a numeric column with summary statistics and a plot, in either
  language, and say which of the two told you something the other hid.
- Audit a data file for values that are legal to the computer and impossible in
  a patient, and quantify how many there are.
- Read a correlation matrix and say which entries you do not believe, with a
  reason that is not "that seems high".
:::

## Why this, here

On Day 1 the first task of the pipeline was *load and inspect*, and the file
obliged: `summary()` showed an age of 109 and a median stay of 66 days, and both
oddities were visible in the output. Today's file is not so helpful. Every
column of `data/diabetes.csv` is numeric, nothing is missing, no summary
function complains, and the defect is still there. It is written as a zero.

## The data

`data/diabetes.csv` holds 768 adults assessed for type 2 diabetes, and it is the
file the rest of the module is built on. Eight measurements taken at a single
screening visit — number of pregnancies, plasma glucose, diastolic blood
pressure, triceps skinfold thickness, serum insulin, body mass index, a pedigree
score summarising family history, and age — and one outcome, `diabetes`,
recorded as `pos` or `neg`.

The scenario is screening. These are measurements a clinic can obtain cheaply in
one visit, and the question is whether they identify who should be sent for a
diagnostic test. That makes it the right case study for the rest of the module:
the cost of a missed case and the cost of an unnecessary referral are plainly
different, and from Day 4 you will be asked to act on that difference rather
than to report accuracy and stop.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2)
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(diabetes)
summary(diabetes)
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
print(diabetes.shape)
diabetes.describe().round(2)
```
:::

Read the `insulin` column of that output before going on. Minimum zero, first
quartile zero, median zero, mean about 75, maximum 846. A serum insulin of zero
is not a low reading; it is not a reading at all.

## What a summary hides, and a plot does not

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
ggplot(diabetes, aes(x = insulin)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 20, boundary = 0) +
  labs(x = "2-hour serum insulin (mu U/ml)", y = "Patients",
       title = "Insulin, as recorded")
```

## Python

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(diabetes["insulin"], bins=range(0, 880, 20))
ax.set_xlabel("2-hour serum insulin (mu U/ml)")
ax.set_ylabel("Patients")
ax.set_title("Insulin, as recorded")
plt.show()
```
:::

The bar at zero is taller than every other bar put together, and it is not a
population of patients with no insulin. The same spike is in `triceps`, smaller
spikes are in `pressure`, `mass` and `glucose`, and none of them is visible in
a table of quartiles unless you are looking for it.

## Task 1 — Count what cannot be true

Count the zeros in every numeric column and express them as a percentage of the
768 rows. Then decide, column by column, which of those zeros could be a real
measurement. One of them can.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
zeros <- diabetes |>
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ sum(______))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_zero") |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n_zero / ______) |>
  arrange(desc(pct))
zeros

insulin_pct <- zeros$pct[zeros$variable == "insulin"]
insulin_pct   # expect 45 to 60
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`.x == 0` is a logical vector, and `sum()` of a logical vector counts the
`TRUE`s. The denominator is the number of rows: `nrow()`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
zeros <- diabetes |>
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ sum(.x == 0))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_zero") |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n_zero / nrow(diabetes)) |>
  arrange(desc(pct))
zeros

insulin_pct <- zeros$pct[zeros$variable == "insulin"]
insulin_pct   # expect 45 to 60
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
num = diabetes.select_dtypes("number")
zeros = (pd.DataFrame({"n_zero": (num == ______).sum()})
         .assign(pct=lambda d: 100 * d["n_zero"] / ______)
         .sort_values("pct", ascending=False))
print(zeros)

insulin_pct = zeros.loc["insulin", "pct"]
print(insulin_pct)   # expect 45 to 60
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
num = diabetes.select_dtypes("number")
zeros = (pd.DataFrame({"n_zero": (num == 0).sum()})
         .assign(pct=lambda d: 100 * d["n_zero"] / len(diabetes))
         .sort_values("pct", ascending=False))
print(zeros)

insulin_pct = zeros.loc["insulin", "pct"]
print(insulin_pct)   # expect 45 to 60
```
:::
:::
:::

Five columns carry zeros that no living adult can produce: `insulin`,
`triceps`, `pressure`, `mass` and `glucose`. The sixth, `pregnant`, is a count
of previous pregnancies, where zero is both common and true. Nothing in the
file distinguishes the two kinds — that distinction is clinical knowledge you
brought with you, and it is the reason a data dictionary is not optional.

## Task 2 — Make the missing values missing

Replace the impossible zeros with `NA` (R) or `np.nan` (Python) in those five
columns, leaving `pregnant` alone, and recompute the mean and median of
`insulin` and `triceps`.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
impossible <- c("glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass")
dia <- diabetes |> mutate(across(all_of(impossible), ~ na_if(.x, ______)))

mean_insulin <- mean(dia$insulin, na.rm = ______)
mean_insulin   # expect 140 to 180
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`na_if(x, y)` returns `NA` wherever `x` equals `y`. Every summary function in R
refuses to average a vector containing `NA` unless you tell it to skip them.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
impossible <- c("glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass")
dia <- diabetes |> mutate(across(all_of(impossible), ~ na_if(.x, 0)))

mean_insulin <- mean(dia$insulin, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_insulin   # expect 140 to 180

dia |>
  summarise(across(all_of(impossible),
                   list(missing = ~ sum(is.na(.x)),
                        mean = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
                        median = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", ".value"), names_sep = "_")
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
impossible = ["glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass"]
dia = diabetes.copy()
dia[impossible] = dia[impossible].replace(______, np.nan)

mean_insulin = dia["insulin"].______
print(mean_insulin)   # expect 140 to 180
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
impossible = ["glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass"]
dia = diabetes.copy()
dia[impossible] = dia[impossible].replace(0, np.nan)

mean_insulin = dia["insulin"].mean()
print(mean_insulin)   # expect 140 to 180

print(dia[impossible].agg(["count", "mean", "median"]).round(1))
```
:::
:::
:::

Compare the two means for `insulin`. The one computed with the zeros in place is
a number that no textbook, no clinician and no laboratory would recognise, and
it was produced by a function that did exactly what it was asked.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `NA` is not a worse answer than a number
Students often resist this step because the dataset "gets smaller". It does not
get smaller; it stops lying. A mean over 363 measured insulins is an estimate of
something. A mean over 768 values of which 405 are a clerical convention is an
estimate of nothing, and it will not announce itself as one.
:::

## Correlation, and what it does with the zeros

The correlation matrix is the usual next step: one number per pair of columns,
telling you which measurements move together.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
num_cols <- c("pregnant", "glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin",
              "mass", "pedigree", "age")
cor_raw <- cor(diabetes[num_cols])
round(cor_raw, 2)
```

## Python

```{python}
num_cols = ["pregnant", "glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin",
            "mass", "pedigree", "age"]
cor_raw = diabetes[num_cols].corr()
cor_raw.round(2)
```
:::

A heatmap makes the structure readable at a glance. There are packages that
draw prettier ones; the point here is that a correlation matrix is just a table
of numbers, so anything that colours a table will do.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
as.data.frame(as.table(cor_raw)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Freq)), size = 2.6) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(limits = c(-1, 1), name = "r") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Correlations, zeros left in") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

## Python

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
im = ax.imshow(cor_raw, vmin=-1, vmax=1, cmap="RdBu_r")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(num_cols)), num_cols, rotation=45, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(num_cols)), num_cols)
for i in range(len(num_cols)):
    for j in range(len(num_cols)):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{cor_raw.iloc[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", size=7)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="r")
ax.set_title("Correlations, zeros left in")
plt.show()
```
:::

The largest off-diagonal entry is `pregnant` with `age`, around 0.74, which
tells you nothing you did not know about how pregnancies accumulate. The next
largest is `insulin` with `triceps`, about 0.47: serum insulin and skin-fold
thickness, more strongly associated with each other than insulin is with
glucose. Hold that thought.

## Task 3 — Recompute the correlations on the measurements that exist

Build the same matrix from `dia` — the frame in which the impossible zeros are
`NA` — using pairwise complete observations, and find the pair whose
correlation changes most.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
cor_na <- cor(dia[num_cols], use = "______")
round(cor_na - cor_raw, 2)

ins_tri <- cor_na["insulin", "triceps"]
ins_tri   # expect 0.0 to 0.3
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`cor()` has a `use =` argument; `"pairwise.complete.obs"` keeps, for each pair
of columns, the rows where both are present. Read its help for what the other
options do — they are not equivalent.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
cor_na <- cor(dia[num_cols], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
round(cor_na - cor_raw, 2)

ins_tri <- cor_na["insulin", "triceps"]
ins_tri   # expect 0.0 to 0.3
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
cor_na = dia[num_cols].______      # pandas skips missing values pairwise by default
print((cor_na - cor_raw).round(2))

ins_tri = cor_na.loc["insulin", "triceps"]
print(ins_tri)   # expect 0.0 to 0.3
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
cor_na = dia[num_cols].corr()
print((cor_na - cor_raw).round(2))

ins_tri = cor_na.loc["insulin", "triceps"]
print(ins_tri)   # expect 0.0 to 0.3
```
:::
:::
:::

## The result that should bother you

The strongest association in the raw matrix is mostly an artefact of the zeros,
and one of the real associations was hidden by them. Both directions, in the
same table.

1. **`insulin` with `triceps` falls from about 0.47 to about 0.17** once the
   zeros are treated as missing. Every one of the 251 rows with a zero skin-fold
   also has a zero insulin, so a quarter of the file sits exactly at the origin
   of that scatter plot. Points at the origin, far below the real values, pull a
   regression line through themselves. The association was between the two
   recording failures, not between the two hormonal quantities.
2. **`triceps` with `mass` rises from about 0.38 to about 0.61.** Skin-fold
   thickness and body mass index measure overlapping things and should agree;
   the zeros were diluting that agreement towards the middle.
3. So the zeros did not add noise. Noise attenuates everything. They *moved*
   correlations, up for pairs that share a missingness pattern and down for
   pairs that do not — and nothing in the output marks which is which.

Here is the control. Take two columns that are independent by construction —
random numbers with plausible means — and knock out exactly the rows that
`insulin` and `triceps` have as zeros. There is no association whatsoever to
find, so whatever correlation appears was manufactured by the zeros.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
set.seed(2025)
fake_insulin <- rnorm(768, mean = 150, sd = 100)
fake_triceps <- rnorm(768, mean = 30,  sd = 10)
cor(fake_insulin, fake_triceps)                      # independent, as drawn

fake_insulin[diabetes$insulin == 0] <- 0
fake_triceps[diabetes$triceps == 0] <- 0
cor(fake_insulin, fake_triceps)                      # same zeros, same artefact
```

## Python

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(2025)
fake_insulin = rng.normal(150, 100, len(diabetes))
fake_triceps = rng.normal(30, 10, len(diabetes))
print(np.corrcoef(fake_insulin, fake_triceps)[0, 1])   # independent, as drawn

fake_insulin[diabetes["insulin"] == 0] = 0
fake_triceps[diabetes["triceps"] == 0] = 0
print(np.corrcoef(fake_insulin, fake_triceps)[0, 1])   # same zeros, same artefact
```
:::

Two variables with nothing to do with each other, correlated at around 0.4
because they were blank on the same patients. The 0.47 you were about to report
is that, plus a little.

## Reflection

1. The zeros are not random: every zero `triceps` is also a zero `insulin`, but
   not the reverse. What kind of clinical process produces nested missingness
   like that, and would you expect the patients it affects to be like the rest?
2. You cannot fix this by deleting the affected rows and you cannot fix it by
   keeping them. Say in one sentence what each choice costs, and what you would
   need to know to choose.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values** (ranges, so a regenerated file does not invalidate them).
Zeros: `insulin` 50–55%, `triceps` 30–35%, `pressure` 4–5%, `mass` 1–2%,
`glucose` under 1%. Mean insulin 75 with zeros, 155–165 without; the median
moves from 0 to about 125. Correlations: `insulin`–`triceps` 0.45–0.50 raw and
0.15–0.20 with zeros as missing; `triceps`–`mass` 0.35–0.40 raw and 0.58–0.63
with zeros as missing. The control lands between 0.35 and 0.49 depending on the
seed.

**Reflection 1.** The nesting says insulin was assayed less often than
anthropometry was measured, and that nobody with a skin-fold reading was
skipped for insulin. That is a clinic workflow, not a patient characteristic —
but the patients who get the full panel are usually the ones someone was
worried about, so the measured subgroup is not a random sample. This is the
hook for @sec-missing-data.

**Reflection 2.** Dropping the 406 affected rows keeps 362 of 768 patients and
biases towards whoever gets fully investigated. Keeping them means modelling a
fiction. Deciding needs the one thing the file cannot tell you: why the value is
absent. Accept any answer that names that; reject "just use the mean", which is
@sec-leakage waiting to happen.

**Common failures.** (1) `sum(.x == 0)` applied to `diabetes` after the
zeros have already been replaced, giving all zeros — tell them to check which
frame they are summarising. (2) In Python, `df.replace(0, np.nan)` across the
whole frame, which also destroys `pregnant`; the task says five columns and the
check does not catch it. (3) `cor()` with default `use = "everything"` on a
frame containing `NA`, which returns a matrix of `NA` rather than an error.

**Timing.** Tasks 1 and 2 take ten minutes together. Protect the last fifteen
for the control, which is the part they remember. If you are short, set Task 3
as reading and run the control from the front.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Does the missingness predict the outcome?
Make a binary column `insulin_missing` and cross-tabulate it against
`diabetes`. If the patients with no insulin result differ in outcome from the
rest, then the fact of measurement carries information — which is either a
clinically real signal about who gets investigated, or a trap, depending on
whether the same process will operate when your model is deployed.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Spearman instead of Pearson
Recompute the raw matrix with `method = "spearman"`. Rank correlation is robust
to outliers, and some people will tell you it therefore handles this. Check
whether the `insulin`–`triceps` artefact survives, and explain the result:
zeros are not outliers, they are ties at the bottom of the ranking.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you have audited this file rather than described it, that you know
how many values in each column are not measurements, and that you can name two
correlations in the published matrix that are wrong and say in which direction.

**Cannot:** anything about what to do with those 405 absent insulins. Replacing
them with a number is easy, and every way of doing it changes a different thing
about the data. That is @sec-missing-data.
